old: I made this mostly because I wanted to learn Devito properly. You hide a structure in a 2D acoustic medium, put a few sources and receivers around it, and try to recover the geometry from the traces. It grew into a versioned testbed with blind challenges and reconstruction scoring.
new: I wanted to learn Devito, so I built an inverse problem around it. The idea is to hide a structure in a 2D acoustic medium and try to reconstruct it from a handful of receiver traces. The v1 release has blind challenges and scoring, too.
reason: Less product-pitch phrasing; explains the problem as a person might explain it.

old: I wanted to know whether you could spot a qualitative change in a dynamical system from the trajectories alone. No equations and no answer key. The paper is my attempt to make that precise enough to test.
new: Can you find structural changes in a dynamical system using only its trajectories, without giving the detector the equations or the transition labels? I tested that on two deterministic systems, then compared its boundaries against separately defined transitions.
reason: Removes theatrical sentence fragments and clarifies the technical claim.

old: LLM changes can get quietly more expensive even when nothing obviously breaks. I wanted CI to be allowed to care about that too.
new: A change to an LLM pipeline can raise the cost per valid answer without breaking its functional tests. Costgate checks that in CI.

old: I came to Imperial because scientific computing is what I had mostly taught myself sideways through all of this. I wanted a year where it was the main subject, not the thing I learned because a problem forced me to.
new: I learned most of my scientific computing on the job, one problem at a time. Imperial is a chance to study the numerical methods behind it rather than picking them up as I go.

old: WaveSleuth is a reproducible inverse-wave playground built around Devito: sparse acoustic observations, inversion baselines, blind challenges, and explicit scores. I started it to learn the solver end to end. The v1 release grew into a small, versioned testbed for reconstruction experiments.
new: I built WaveSleuth to learn Devito by implementing an inverse problem from start to finish. A 2D acoustic model generates traces from a hidden medium, and the inversion tries to reconstruct it from sparse observations. The v1 release adds blind challenges, scoring, and checks that the results can be reproduced.
reason: Abstract-like opening replaced with what the code does and why it exists.

old: The actual v1.0 loop. Sources and receivers are sparse on purpose. Ambiguity is part of the game.
new: This is the v1.0 workflow. The small number of sources and receivers leaves room for ambiguous reconstructions.
reason: Removes the slogan-like last sentence.

old: I wanted to know whether a detector could pick up structural change without being told what kind of change it should expect. I kept the governing equations, regime labels, and transition definitions away from it and only gave it trajectories across an ordered parameter sweep.
new: The detector gets full-state trajectories and the order of a parameter sweep, but no equations, regime labels, or transition definitions. I wanted to see whether it could still identify a structural boundary.
reason: Makes the information barrier clearer, cuts vague framing.

old: The qualitative boundary is computed separately with model specific information and only brought back at evaluation. On the two deterministic benchmark families in the paper, using multivariate/full-state trajectories, the structural boundary appears earlier than the separately defined qualitative boundary. No general-purpose bifurcation guarantee is claimed.
new: I defined the qualitative transitions separately and withheld them until evaluation. In both deterministic benchmark families, the boundary detected from multivariate/full-state trajectories appeared earlier. That is a result on two systems, not a general result about every dynamical system.
reason: Replaces legalistic caveat with a plain statement of scope.

old: Before a learned equation of state goes anywhere near a CFD or VLE solver, make it pass a few cheap physical consistency checks.
new: C1–C4 check monotonicity, mechanical stability, phase consistency, and sound speed before the surrogate is used in a solver.
reason: Turns generic advice into the actual tests.

old: An LLM change can get more expensive while all the normal tests still pass. The API returns, the output looks fine, and the bill quietly moves in the wrong direction. Costgate gives that kind of regression a place in CI.
new: A code change can leave an LLM pipeline’s answers unchanged while raising the cost per valid answer. Costgate compares a candidate run against a baseline in CI and checks it against a policy.
reason: Removes familiar metaphor and personification; adds concrete operation.

reason: Specifies the output without self-conscious product positioning.

old: This was supposed to be a surrogate model paper. It turned into a negative result when the learned pressure surface and its derivatives failed in the regions the VLE solver actually needed. That failure became the useful part.

old: A compact benchmark for checking whether learned thermodynamic surrogates still satisfy basic physical constraints before they are trusted inside VLE, CFD, or related solver workflows.
new: Four consistency checks for learned pure-fluid equations of state, including monotonicity, compressibility, the Clapeyron relation, and sound speed.
reason: Substitutes details for generic benefit language, preserves pure-fluid scope.
